title: A fault under the island
teaches: How geologists showed that the South Whidbey Island fault is active with no earthquake on record: lidar that sees through forest, trenches across scarps, and dates from the layers

blocks.text: Written records in the Puget Sound region go back only to the 1830s, and the region’s big twentieth-century and modern earthquakes, in 1949, 1965 and 2001, were all deep, inside the subducting plate. None of them came from the faults near the surface. Yet the US Geological Survey lists several shallow faults across the lowland as active and dangerous. One of them, the **South Whidbey Island fault**, runs from near Port Townsend across the south end of Whidbey, past Mukilteo and on toward Woodinville.

A fault can still be dangerous even if no one has ever seen it have an earthquake. Lesson 18 gives the reason to worry: a locked fault stores strain for centuries and then lets it go. A few hundred years of quiet means nothing. What is needed is a record that goes back thousands of years, and the ground itself keeps one.

blocks.caption: The Puget Lowland, with the approximate line of the South Whidbey Island fault zone. It is a zone of several strands kilometres wide, not one line.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: The region’s recent big quakes were deep; the shallow faults have no written history.
The South Whidbey Island fault runs from near Port Townsend across south Whidbey toward Woodinville.
Only a record thousands of years long can show whether such a fault is active.

blocks.text: The first step is to find where the fault reaches the surface. In the Puget Lowland that is hard: the ground is covered in dense forest, and the glaciers smeared everything about 16,000 years ago. A fault that has broken the surface since then should have left a **scarp**, a small step in the ground, but under trees a step one or two metres high is invisible.

**Lidar** solved this. An aircraft fires tens to hundreds of thousands of laser pulses a second at the ground and times their echoes. Most bounce off leaves, but some find gaps and reach the ground, and software keeps only those last echoes, giving a map of the bare earth with the forest removed (lesson 17). In 1996 the USGS tested lidar on Whidbey Island, and from 1999 a consortium of local governments and the USGS flew it across the Puget Lowland. Geologists started to see things nobody had seen: fresh-looking scarps cutting across glacial landforms, across Bainbridge Island on the Seattle fault and along the South Whidbey Island fault zone and others.[^lidar] Those scarps are younger than the ice, so the faults that made them have broken the surface within the last 16,000 years.

blocks.caption: A fault scarp revealed by lidar: a sharp step across smooth glacial landforms, invisible under the forest.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: A fault that breaks the surface leaves a scarp, hidden under forest.
Lidar keeps the echoes from the ground and maps the bare earth, revealing scarps younger than the ice.

blocks.text: A scarp says the fault has moved since the ice left. To learn when, and how often, geologists dig a **trench** across it with a backhoe, a few metres deep, and log its walls layer by layer. Sediment is laid down flat, as Steno said (lesson 1). Where an earthquake breaks the ground, every layer that exists at that moment is cut and offset by the fault. Layers laid down afterward lie across the break unbroken. So each earthquake is pinned between the youngest layer it broke and the oldest one it did not.

blocks.caption: A trench wall across a fault, simplified, from a made-up history of the kind trench logs record. Each earthquake lifts the left side about a metre.

blocks.text: Dating the layers closes the case. Peat, charcoal and plant remains in them can be dated by radiocarbon (lesson 8), which gives each earthquake a window of a few centuries. Trenches across the South Whidbey Island fault zone from 1999 through the 2000s showed the ground broken at least four times since the ice left, the latest within the last 3,000 years. Together with the lidar scarps and with marsh deposits at Cultus Bay on south Whidbey, where tidal mud changes abruptly to peat or back, a sign that the ground jumped up or down in a moment, as at Restoration Point in the Seattle branch, that is enough: the fault is active, and it can produce earthquakes of around magnitude 7, shallow and close to many people.

So the absence of a written record says little. On the scale of a fault, 190 years is a moment. The record that matters is written in layers of soil, and it says the South Whidbey Island fault will break again, at a time nobody can yet predict.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: A trench across a scarp shows which layers each quake broke and which lie over the break unbroken.
Radiocarbon dates of the layers bracket each earthquake.
The South Whidbey Island fault has broken several times since the ice left; it is active.

blocks.caption: Five questions on the South Whidbey Island fault
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: Why does the lack of a recorded earthquake not show that the fault is safe?
choices: Written records cover less than 200 years, far shorter than the time between quakes
The fault is too small to matter
items.why: A locked fault can stay quiet for centuries while it stores strain.

items.ask: Why do geologists use lidar to find scarps in the Puget Lowland?
choices: It maps the bare ground under the forest
It sees deep into the rock
items.why: The last echoes of the laser pulses come from the ground, so the trees can be removed.

items.ask: A scarp cuts across glacial landforms. What does that tell you?
choices: The fault has broken the surface since the ice left, about 16,000 years ago
The fault is older than the ice
items.why: The landforms are about 16,000 years old, and the scarp cuts them, so it is younger.

items.ask: In a trench wall, a quake broke the gravel and silt but not the peat above them. When was it?
choices: After the silt was laid down and before the peat
items.why: It broke every layer that existed then, and the peat came later.

items.ask: How are the layers in a trench dated?
choices: Radiocarbon in peat, charcoal and plant remains
items.why: Organic remains in the layers can be radiocarbon dated, giving windows for each quake.

summary: **No written record means little.** It covers less than 200 years.
**The South Whidbey Island fault is shallow.** It runs from near Port Townsend toward Woodinville.
**Faults that break the surface leave scarps.** Forest hides them.
**Lidar strips the forest away.** It revealed scarps younger than the ice.
**Trenches read the history.** Broken layers are older than a quake, unbroken ones younger.
**Radiocarbon dates the quakes.** Several since the ice left.
**The fault is active.** It can make quakes around magnitude 7.

lidar.title: The Puget Sound Lidar Consortium
lidar.text: The Puget Sound Lidar Consortium, formed in the late 1990s by the USGS, NASA, local counties and cities, flew much of the lowland with airborne lidar between 1996 and the late 2000s and made the data public. The first results, including the scarp across Bainbridge Island at Toe Jam Hill, were published by Ralph Haugerud, Brian Sherrod and colleagues in 2003.
